A sloven is a person who is habitually dirty, untidy, and careless — in how they look, how they live, and often in how they work. If you call someone a sloven, you are saying that messiness and neglect are not accidents for them — they are a way of life.

This is the most important thing to understand. A sloven is not someone who had a rough week and let the dishes pile up. It is not someone whose hair was messy on one bad morning. Everyone has untidy days.

A sloven is someone for whom this is the norm. Their clothes are almost always stained or wrinkled. Their living space is almost always in disorder. Their personal hygiene is almost always neglected. If you visit them on Monday, the place is a mess. If you visit on Friday, it is still a mess — perhaps a worse one. This is simply how they are, day after day.
The Three Areas Where It Shows

The word "sloven" can apply to one or all of the following:

1. Personal appearance
A sloven tends to look unkempt. Unwashed hair, dirty fingernails, stained or rumpled clothing, body odor — the basic acts of grooming and dressing that most people do without thinking are simply not priorities for a sloven. They either don't notice or don't care.

2. Living space and surroundings
A sloven's home, room, or desk often reflects the same neglect. Dust, clutter, unwashed dishes, clothes scattered on the floor — there is a general air of things being left wherever they fell, with no attempt to bring order.

3. Work and effort
The word can also describe a person who is careless and sloppy in their work — someone who rushes through tasks without attention to quality, makes avoidable errors, and treats precision or thoroughness as someone else's problem. Here, the "messiness" is in the output of their labor rather than in their physical environment.

What makes someone a sloven isn't simply that their life is messy — it is that they let it be messy. The word implies a person who either does not notice the disorder around them or does not think it worth the effort to change it. There is a certain laziness or indifference built into the word.

This is what separates a sloven from, say, someone who is simply overwhelmed or going through a difficult period. A sloven's disorderliness comes not from circumstances but from character — from a settled, ingrained carelessness.

Sloven is a strongly disapproving word. Using it is an insult. It implies not just that a person is messy, but that this messiness reflects poorly on them as a person — that they lack self-respect, discipline, or consideration for others.

The word also has a slightly old-fashioned or literary feel. You are more likely to encounter it in a classic novel, a formal essay, or as a deliberately pointed insult than in everyday casual conversation. Its adjective form, slovenly, is more commonly used today (as in "slovenly habits" or "a slovenly appearance"), but the noun form — sloven — is the sharper, more direct form, applied to the person themselves.
How It Differs from Similar Words

• A slob is the closest modern equivalent and is used more casually and informally. A slob is messy and lazy; a sloven carries the same meaning but sounds more deliberate and cutting, and often emphasizes the habitual, ingrained nature of the problem.
  • Slob is more American and colloquial; sloven is more formal and literary.
  • A boor is someone who is rude and unmannered but not necessarily dirty; a sloven's failing is specifically about physical cleanliness and orderliness.
  • A wastrel or layabout is lazy but not necessarily untidy; a sloven's laziness specifically expresses itself through neglect of cleanliness and neatness.

• "His mother despaired of him — a grown man living like a sloven, with week-old takeaway containers on every surface and no clean clothes to his name."
  • "She had hoped for a diligent assistant, not this sloven who turned in careless, error-riddled reports and thought nothing of it."
  • "The neighbors whispered that old Mr. Jarvis had become a complete sloven since his wife passed — the garden overgrown, the curtains drawn at noon, the man himself unwashed."

If you had to summarize in one sentence: a sloven is a person for whom dirt, disorder, and carelessness are not occasional lapses but a defining, habitual way of being — in their appearance, their home, or their work, or all three at once. The word judges them for it, implying that this is not misfortune but a failure of will and self-respect.
